An Open Letter to Russell Brand’s Lawyers
Dear Sirs and Dames,
Your client Russell Brand is not in prison because the British state discovered a sudden interest in the safety of women. The UK is globally infamous for the official coverup of thousands of young women raped by grooming gangs who were then sheltered from justice by London.

No, Russell is in prison because he told millions of people the truth that the British government and powerful figures like Bill Gates and Pfizer violated and continue to violate the Nuremberg Code and international laws on informed consent.

That’s why the government needed him gone, and the story of his prosecution makes his setup patently obvious.

Any defense of Russell that does not use this context to his benefit will struggle to win. The case is political and, like the January 6th political prisoners, Russell is likely to stay in jail until a political change sweeps the UK. The defense in this case should aim to support and provoke that change. Russell’s trial is a test of the government’s legitimacy during COVID, the lack of which can only be exposed if we press the deeper truths.

Look at the motives and timeline in the cited brief below. What am I missing?

Dame Caroline Dinenage spent the pandemic as the minister for Online Harms.

She was the minister for the speech law.

She’s married to a senior military information warfare officer.

She chaired the controversial Commons subcommittee on Online Harms and Disinformation.

On September 12th, 2023 she stood in the House for that law’s return.

Four days later a public broadcaster whose coverage is steered by Parliament put a years-long sexual file on Russell.

The UK now leads the free world in the number of arrests for social media posts.

The police had no formal reports on Russell. Instead they recruited journalists, in a replay of the Julian Assange setup.

Dinenage then wrote the platforms, including an American company, and asked them to join YouTube in cutting his income and asked whether Elon Musk had personally intervened. There were still no charges. Nineteen months later the Crown Prosecution Service charged Brand and said the file had come from that broadcast. A judge has now given him ten years and six months, and in the first paragraph of the remarks credited the same broadcast with bringing the complainants forward.

This is a scandal. The government is actually trying to take credit for a legal breach of ethics for which it would ordinarily have to apologize.

It’s a manufactured case. It was built to solve a political problem for the Establishment, not the people.

The problem was that Russell was telling the truth about government crimes against humanity.

Lawyer Ian Winter KC already told Mr Justice Bennathan that Channel 4, Hardcash Productions, and the Sunday Times had poisoned the well. The judge let the trial go on. What follows is an exploration into the nature of that poison and the depth of the well.

Who needed him silent? What had he been saying? Who made the film? Who wrote the letters? And how was the rape file assembled from an empty police blotter?

Here in the United States we are actively monitoring this case and preparing to file it with the Department Of State’s Human Rights Desk. I will be asking the State Department to request a formal meeting with the British Ambassador.

How can we be helpful?

Here’s what I think is necessary going forward. We lost the media argument. Bennathan ruled that an impartial jury could be found, and the Court of Appeal will likely not revisit that. So let’s use the argument the trial never made:

Three days after Channel 4 aired its film, with no complaint on file and no charge, the chair of a Commons committee wrote to X, Rumble and TikTok and asked them to cut off Russell Brand’s income. The same Dame Caroline Dinenage had spent the pandemic answering to Parliament for the Counter Disinformation Unit, and she told the House that the platforms had agreed that “no user or company should directly profit” from COVID misinformation. She put that same word, profit, to the platforms in her letters about your client. That is the state moving against a man before any court spoke, and you can show it from her own letters and her own answers to Parliament. Put the CPS’s words beside it: the charges followed “the broadcast.” Put the judge’s words beside both: the broadcast “empowered” the women to come forward. Then ask the Court of Appeal the question your jury never heard. Why do these complaints exist?

The publicity complaint asked the court to ignore his rough press treatment.

An abuse-of-process complaint puts the state on trial for how their case was made. Make political speech your core argument, and make them answer it. The brief below adds citations.

If BCL or Cloth Fair Chambers are no longer on the case, please give this to whoever is and please let me know who is now on point.

Robin Hood is back in jail. What are we going to do about it?

Yours faithfully,

Leland

November 16th, 2026
R. Leland Lehrman
641 Harlemville Road
Hillsdale, NY 12529 USA
lelandatwork@fund-balance.com
+1-519-291-2269
Signal and Telegram
Notice of appeal against conviction is due December 3rd, 2026. The notice against sentence is due December 7th.
Why they needed Russell Brand silenced
The Nuremberg Code is not a metaphor. Principle one is voluntary, informed consent.[1] A person cannot give informed consent to a medical procedure if the state hides the risks, punishes the asking of questions, and makes the job, the travel, and the ordinary life of the unvaccinated into a punishment. That is what the British government did. It locked down the country. It pushed an experimental product on a healthy population without the informed consent the Code requires. It treated dissent as a policing problem. It ran a Counter Disinformation Unit inside the culture department, with privileged access to the platforms,[2] and it put soldiers from the Army’s 77th Brigade onto the domestic information war.[3] Journalists, members of Parliament, and scientists who questioned lockdowns, vaccine passports, and the vaccination of children were logged.[4] The Daily Telegraph reported on September 1st, 2023 that the UK intelligence community had been inside that unit since 2019.[5]
Those are crimes against the person and crimes against the peace of a free people. They are the same species of offence the Nuremberg tribunal named when it said that medical experiments without informed consent are a crime against humanity.[6] Britain did not put people on tables in a camp. It put a nation under a medical order, denied it the information required for informed consent, and used the law and the platforms to punish anyone who said so.
Russell Brand said so.
Here are the violated laws he pointed to. Where was the Crown Prosecution Service then?
Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984, s.45E: regulations under ss.45B and 45C may not require a person to undergo medical treatment, which includes vaccination.
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11, para 87: an adult of sound mind decides which treatment to undergo, and consent must be obtained before treatment interfering with bodily integrity.

Re T (Adult: Refusal of Treatment) [1993] Fam 95: a competent adult may refuse treatment for any reason or none.

Re B (Adult: Refusal of Medical Treatment) [2002] EWHC 429 (Fam): a competent patient’s refusal must be respected.

St George’s Healthcare NHS Trust v S [1999] Fam 26: treating a competent adult without consent is a trespass to the person.

Common law of battery: touching a person without valid consent is unlawful.

Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Article 8: respect for private life, which includes bodily integrity.

Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1, Article 3: no inhuman or degrading treatment.

Human Rights Act 1998, s.6: public authorities must act compatibly with those rights.

Medicines for Human Use (Clinical Trials) Regulations 2004, Schedule 1, Part 3: informed consent, and the right to withdraw without detriment.

Mental Capacity Act 2005, s.1: a person is presumed to have capacity, and an unwise decision does not show incapacity.

Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, reg. 11: care providers must have the person’s consent before providing care or treatment.

International Criminal Court Act 2001, s.51 (with s.50): crimes against humanity and war crimes, including unlawful medical experiments, are offences in England and Wales.

International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 7: no one may be subjected without free consent to medical or scientific experimentation (a UK treaty obligation).

Unfortunately, he was their product first.

BBC Radio 2. Channel 4. Big Brother’s Big Mouth. Hollywood. They made him famous as a sexual clown and sold that persona for years. Then he left the tent and took the audience with him. He talked, every day, to millions, about vaccine mandates as an assault on the body and on informed consent, about Pfizer’s profits, about Albert Bourla calling questioners criminals, about the World Health Organization writing YouTube’s rules while taking money from the American government and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, about Gates saying out of his own mouth that the shots do not stop infection and do not last, about the money Gates made on BioNTech.[7] May 7th, 2021: Vaccine Gold Rush. September 16th, 2021: mandates. June 9th, 2022: Pfizer at Davos. October 15th, 2022: YouTube struck him for saying Pfizer had not tested transmission. January and February 2023: the Twitter Files, the White House asking Facebook to remove “often true content,” Fauci and Gates and the profit.

A working-class, left-coded, funny, spiritual man with 11.3 million people on X[8] and 6.6 million on YouTube,[9] inside British jurisdiction, naming the crime against informed consent. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is an American problem. Brand was a British one. They already owned his sexual past. They had sold it. They did not need to invent his sins. They needed to compromise him with them.

Dame Caroline Dinenage was the officer in charge.

After she sets up Britain’s Censorship laws, Dinenage was promoted to Dame. That’s how you know this is political. In America, we call it failing upwards. Here’s the timeline:

January 2018 to February 2020: Minister of State at the Department of Health and Social Care. February 13th, 2020 to September 2021: Minister of State for Digital and Culture, the minister for Online Harms, with the Online Safety Bill in her hands through the whole of the medical order.[10] The Counter Disinformation Unit sat in that department. She answered Parliament for it.[11] 2022: made a Dame as the MP first responsible for that Bill.[12] May 2023: elected Chair of the Culture, Media and Sport Committee.[13] From May 17th, 2023 to May 30th, 2024 she also chaired its subcommittee on Online Harms and Disinformation.[14]

Her husband is Mark Lancaster, Baron Lancaster of Kimbolton. https://t.co/SklYy4Lwv8 states, in his own biography: “He is married to Caroline Dinenage.”[15] He has been reported as deputy commander of the 77th Brigade, the Army’s information-warfare formation, from 2018 to July 2020.[16] He held senior reserve posts through 2023. The household is health ministry, online harms, soldiers on the domestic information war, and the committee that cut Brand’s money.

On September 12th, 2023, four days before the film aired, she stood for the Online Safety Bill’s return. She called the regulator world class. She said the Bill would clear illegal content from the internet.[17] Then the film dropped. Then she wrote the platforms.

The people who made the film

The Sunday Times has now told us who they were, in their own celebration of the verdict.[18]

Rosamund Urwin, now chief news correspondent of the Sunday Times, began speaking to comedy and television sources in January 2019. Charlotte Wace of The Times later took the American years. Paul Morgan-Bentley, head of investigations, is named on the paper’s own account of the joint work. Ben Taylor, editor of the Sunday Times, stood over Urwin after the verdict. The Times says the investigation took four years and that in autumn 2022 Channel 4’s Dispatches formally began collaborating with the Sunday Times.[18] Channel 4’s own later review says development of the programme was formally commissioned in December 2019.[19] That is the same month the medical order was about to swallow the country, and the same years Brand was using the audience Channel 4 had given him to name the order and the destruction of informed consent.

The film was made by Hardcash Productions for Channel 4 Dispatches. Hardcash says so on its own site.[20] Ian Winter KC named Hardcash in written submissions. He called the programme a work of fiction. He told the judge that the anonymised women on screen were depicted by actors. He said the conduct of Channel 4, Hardcash, and the Sunday Times in publishing anonymous allegations was unlawful and criminal.[21]

Channel 4 is publicly owned. Its remit is set by Parliament. This was not a private scoop. It was a public corporation, a Times investigation begun in 2019, a production company, and a years-long build, dropped in the week the Online Safety Bill came back and the minister for the speech law wrote the platforms.

The week they spent the file

Saturday, September 16th, 2023. Channel 4 airs Russell Brand: In Plain Sight: Dispatches. Four anonymous women. Actors on screen for the anonymous parts, as Winter told the court.[24]

Sunday, September 17th. Channel 4 News, Anja Popp:

“There have been no formal reports to the police in connection with the allegations against Russell Brand, although in the last hour Scotland Yard said they would be speaking again to the Sunday Times and Channel 4 to ensure any victims of crime they had spoken to, were aware of how to report any criminal allegations to police.”[25]

Read that again. The Metropolitan Police had no formal reports. They went back to Rosamund Urwin’s paper and to Channel 4 so the people those journalists had already used could be walked into a criminal complaint.

The same day Channel 4 announced an internal investigation. It published a Metropolitan Police mailbox for complainants and invited more stories to Dispatches@Channel4.co.uk.[26]

Tuesday, September 19th. YouTube cuts his income under a “creator responsibility policy.” No charge.[27] The same day Dame Caroline writes Dr Theo Bertram at TikTok: confirm whether Brand monetises, including videos relating to the accusations. TikTok replies that he has never been in the Creator Fund.[28]

Wednesday, September 20th. She writes Linda Yaccarino at X Corp. Will X join YouTube in suspending his ability to earn money. Has Elon Musk personally intervened in any decision on his status. She quotes Musk: “Of course. They don’t like competition.”[29] She writes Chris Pavlovski at Rumble the same ask.[30] She wrote Meta the same day; Meta replied on September 29th.[31] There is still no charge.

Thursday, September 21st. Pavlovski calls the letter extremely disturbing. He says it is deeply inappropriate and dangerous that the UK Parliament would attempt to control who may speak on a platform or earn a living from doing so, and that singling out an individual and demanding his ban is even more disturbing given the absence of any connection between the allegations and his content on Rumble.[32]

Monday, September 25th. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, Met Central Specialist Crime: several allegations received following the media reports; anyone who believes they may have been a victim, no matter how long ago, should come forward.[33]

April 4th, 2025. First charges. Nineteen months. Jaswant Narwal, CPS:

“We carefully reviewed the evidence after a police investigation into allegations made following the broadcast of a Channel 4, Sunday Times and Times investigation in September 2023.”[35]

December 23rd, 2025. Lionel Idan, CPS, adds a 2009 rape and a 2009 sexual assault, two more women. Those later charges become two of the four counts the jury convicted. The nine-year rape term sits on a count that did not exist until twenty-seven months after Dinenage’s letters.[36]

November 5th, 2026. Jury: guilty of one rape and three sexual assaults; not guilty of two rapes and one attempted indecent assault. Remanded. David Roberts, CPS:

“The women did not report the offences to police at the time. ... The broadcast of a television programme about Brand in September 2023 prompted them, independently and for their own reasons, to come forward.”

“Given the time that has passed, the evidence available in this case was limited.”[37]

The prosecutors in court were Riel Karmy-Jones KC, Suki Dhadda, and Katie Bacon.[38] They told the jury a pattern story because, as the CPS then admitted in writing, the evidence was limited.

November 9th, 2026. Mr Justice Joel Bennathan. Ten years six months. Paragraph 1: the 2023 documentary and Times articles “empowered a number of women to come forward.” Paragraph 5: “I disregard the allegations in the documentary.” Paragraph 16: “I accept there is no sound evidential basis for me to conclude you pose a risk for the future.”[39]

They needed the film to create the case. They disowned the film as evidence. They locked him anyway. They found no future danger. His wife and children are in that sentence with him.

This is how a state fixes a speech problem. It does not answer the Nuremberg point on informed consent. It does not debate Gates or Pfizer or consent. It uses an old sexual file, fills a police book from a journalist’s list, cuts the man’s money from a committee chair’s desk, waits, charges, and calls the result justice.

What we can do now

The notice of appeal against conviction is due December 3rd, 2026. Against sentence, December 7th. Criminal Appeal Act 1968, section 18. Criminal Procedure Rules 39.2.[40]

We ran prejudicial publicity. Now we run state conflict of interest, abuse of process, and prosecutorial ethics violations.

The letters are not a culture-committee enquiry. They are an Online Harms instrument written by the minister for the speech law, four days after she pushed that law, against the man who was using a mass audience to name the medical order and the destruction of informed consent. Abuse of process. A state-created prosecution.

Here’s what we need:

The Met began with no formal reports and went to Urwin’s paper and to Channel 4. Demand every contact between Met officers and Sunday Times, Times, Channel 4, and Hardcash journalists and producers from the first of September 2023. Demand the September 17th instruction. Demand unused material on how each of the four convicted counts’ complainants first reached police. Demand every fee, reconstruction contract, appearance payment, and later book or newspaper deal in that chain. Winter already put the actors on the record. Get the contracts.

The CPS and the judge have both written that the broadcast created the complainants. Put Narwal’s April 4th, 2025 sentence, Roberts’s November 5th, 2026 sentence, and Bennathan paragraph 1 on one page. That page is the origin of the case, in the state’s own words.

Add Rumble’s letter and Pavlovski’s refusal. So do Dinenage’s offices, in order: Health, Online Harms, Dame for the speech law, Chair of Online Harms and Disinformation, the letters of September 19th and 20th. text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

Delhi Police asks IFF for records in its investigation of the takedown reports sent to X in its name. IFF has replied and is disclosing what it furnished.

On 13 November 2026, the Cyber Cell of the Delhi Police Crime Branch sent the Internet Freedom Foundation a notice under Section 94 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). It asks for IFF's records on the takedown reports that were sent to X in the name of a senior Delhi Police officer, and that sought the removal of our account and six of our posts. IFF replied on 14 November 2026 and furnished the records.

We are publishing the notice and our reply because our community should know when the police ask us for information, what was asked and what we gave. IFF welcomes the investigation and calls on the Delhi Police to make its findings public.

What has happened

Between 29 October and 3 November 2026, IFF with @SFLCin  and @geoblockedindia received two notices purportedly to be issued on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). X then forwarded to us two "Illegal Content Reports" submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime). On 6 November, at the hearing of our petition before the Delhi High Court, X said that the email from which the reports were submitted appears to be fake, and that it had complained to the Delhi Police. The Court recorded this and disposed of our petition, with liberty to return if any action is taken against our account or posts.

The notice is issued in FIR No. 268/2026, registered on 5 November 2026 at Police Station Crime Branch under Sections 336(3), 204 and 340(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. These cover forgery for the purpose of cheating, personating a public servant, using a forged document or electronic record as genuine, and cheating by personation using a computer resource. The notice says the FIR concerns "unauthorized takedown requests sent to X" by someone impersonating a senior officer of the Crime Branch or another police authority.

It requires IFF to produce three things:

1) The complete trail of emails, with attachments and full headers, about the notices in the RSS's name and the takedown requests, from X or anyone else.
2) The posts we made on X on the subject, and the posts in which we were tagged.
3) Certified copies of the applications we filed before the Delhi High Court, and of its order.

It asks for a certificate under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), and for the original emails and files to be preserved.

What we furnished

Our reply went by email on 14 November, and we told the police that a printed set would follow by speed post. It carries an 87-page set of annexures and a signed certificate:

1) Fifteen emails, printed with their full headers and attachments. These are the four emails from the Proton Mail address that sent the two notices, our two replies, our email to the RSS at its official address, and the four emails from X, three of which enclose the two reports. The set also has four emails with, who received the same notices and wrote to us about them. That person is identified in them only by the account's handle and its own email address as we lack knowledge about them otherwise.

2) A list of the ten posts we published on the subject between 30 October and 6 November, with links, times and text. We did not compile posts by other users who tagged us. The other users' posts named in the reports are listed in the reports themselves.

3) A certificate under Section 63(4) of the BSA, with the hash values of the files.

The legal notice dated 3 November that our counsel served on the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), in the redacted form we published on 4 November.

On the High Court record, we said that certified copies can be obtained from the Registry, and that the Delhi Police has already been served with our petition and applications. We also told the police what we have said in public since 30 October. We do not know who sent the two notices and cannot say that they came from the RSS. We wrote to the RSS at its official address on 30 October and marked it on our reply of 1 November. It has not responded. We gave the records that bear on the notices and the reports. Much of this, including the notices, our replies, the reports and the legal notice, was already public.

IFF's position

IFF is the target of these reports and someone used the name of one of the most senior officers of the Delhi Police to try to have our account and posts removed. We said on 6 November that it is for the Delhi Police to investigate who made the reports and to say so publicly. An investigation has begun, and we have cooperated with it.

Section 94 of the BNSS allows a police officer to require a person, by written order, to produce documents needed for an investigation. We complied because this notice is confined to the records of an episode in which we are the affected party. The material was furnished without prejudice to our rights, including the liberty the High Court gave us. If we are asked for anything more, we will look at each request on its own terms, take legal advice and tell you what we can.

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

The case stems from a pig butchering victim who allegedly lost $1.7M of BTC, USDT, DOGE & SOL in May 2025.

Gate froze his entire account, which held roughly $3M at the time and about $1.5M today.

bc1quzw & bc1qtu66z were reported as alibarbit[.]bit, the same scam named in Indian LE's press release.

xxxkeym bridged 50 BTC into Merlin on March 28, 2024, over a year before the alleged May 2025 theft.

Separately on July 15, 2025 xxxkeym had a 7 BTC private key compromise theft which was reported to local police and also SlowMist was engaged. His stolen funds flowed to Wasabi. 

This is embarrassing incompetence by Indian LE, who seem incapable of reviewing basic blockchain data.

Indian LE, the prosecutor and the judge all signed off on this, Gate froze the account, and LE did a full press release about it recently, while the real victim here (the Gate user) hasn't had access to his funds for nearly 16 months.

3. What is the meaning of a P2P exchange if, after tax deduction, withdrawals are still blocked by banks and flagged by authorities?

4. Is CoinDCX registered as a third party app with Indian banks, or why is there no direct coordination with banks to prevent such issues?

—> If this problem is not addressed with a clear and transparent solution, then users will be forced to assume that CoinDCX’s P2P services are unsafe or misleading.

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. 🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

text:
Can a software-based video compression method be patented in India?

We look at Huawei’s Patent No. 558691 and assess it in light of India’s Computer Related Inventions (CRI) Guidelines.

What Do the 2025 CRI Guidelines Say?

The 2025 CRI Guidelines place greater emphasis on an invention's technical effect. This means software-based methods may be assessed based on the technical results they produce. This technical-effect test aligns with European standards, which the Parliament explicitly rejected in 2004 to prevent a “monopoly of multinationals”.

Does producing a technical result change the nature of the underlying invention? No, it does not.

Huawei’s patent still claims a way of processing information through software, via an algorithm, not a new hardware component. This raises concerns about whether the 2025 Guidelines weaken the legislative intent behind Section 3(k) of the Patents Act, 1970.

Transparency Matters

When a patent is granted, the reasoning behind the decision matters. In this case, the patent was granted without a hearing, and the Patent Controller’s detailed reasoning is not available on the Indian Patent Office website.

Without this reasoning, it is difficult to understand how the Section 3(k) objection was addressed or why the patent was considered eligible for grant.

“Say No to Software Patents” has long been https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position. Through our Patent Watch series, we examine software patents in India and their implications for software freedom.

Delhi Police asks IFF for records in its investigation of the takedown reports sent to X in its name. IFF has replied and is disclosing what it furnished.

On 13 November 2026, the Cyber Cell of the Delhi Police Crime Branch sent the Internet Freedom Foundation a notice under Section 94 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). It asks for IFF's records on the takedown reports that were sent to X in the name of a senior Delhi Police officer, and that sought the removal of our account and six of our posts. IFF replied on 14 November 2026 and furnished the records.

We are publishing the notice and our reply because our community should know when the police ask us for information, what was asked and what we gave. IFF welcomes the investigation and calls on the Delhi Police to make its findings public.

What has happened

Between 29 October and 3 November 2026, IFF with @SFLCin  and @geoblockedindia received two notices purportedly to be issued on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). X then forwarded to us two "Illegal Content Reports" submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime). On 6 November, at the hearing of our petition before the Delhi High Court, X said that the email from which the reports were submitted appears to be fake, and that it had complained to the Delhi Police. The Court recorded this and disposed of our petition, with liberty to return if any action is taken against our account or posts.

The notice is issued in FIR No. 268/2026, registered on 5 November 2026 at Police Station Crime Branch under Sections 336(3), 204 and 340(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. These cover forgery for the purpose of cheating, personating a public servant, using a forged document or electronic record as genuine, and cheating by personation using a computer resource. The notice says the FIR concerns "unauthorized takedown requests sent to X" by someone impersonating a senior officer of the Crime Branch or another police authority.

It requires IFF to produce three things:

1) The complete trail of emails, with attachments and full headers, about the notices in the RSS's name and the takedown requests, from X or anyone else.
2) The posts we made on X on the subject, and the posts in which we were tagged.
3) Certified copies of the applications we filed before the Delhi High Court, and of its order.

It asks for a certificate under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), and for the original emails and files to be preserved.

What we furnished

Our reply went by email on 14 November, and we told the police that a printed set would follow by speed post. It carries an 87-page set of annexures and a signed certificate:

1) Fifteen emails, printed with their full headers and attachments. These are the four emails from the Proton Mail address that sent the two notices, our two replies, our email to the RSS at its official address, and the four emails from X, three of which enclose the two reports. The set also has four emails with, who received the same notices and wrote to us about them. That person is identified in them only by the account's handle and its own email address as we lack knowledge about them otherwise.

2) A list of the ten posts we published on the subject between 30 October and 6 November, with links, times and text. We did not compile posts by other users who tagged us. The other users' posts named in the reports are listed in the reports themselves.

3) A certificate under Section 63(4) of the BSA, with the hash values of the files.

The legal notice dated 3 November that our counsel served on the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), in the redacted form we published on 4 November.

On the High Court record, we said that certified copies can be obtained from the Registry, and that the Delhi Police has already been served with our petition and applications. We also told the police what we have said in public since 30 October. We do not know who sent the two notices and cannot say that they came from the RSS. We wrote to the RSS at its official address on 30 October and marked it on our reply of 1 November. It has not responded. We gave the records that bear on the notices and the reports. Much of this, including the notices, our replies, the reports and the legal notice, was already public.

IFF's position

IFF is the target of these reports and someone used the name of one of the most senior officers of the Delhi Police to try to have our account and posts removed. We said on 6 November that it is for the Delhi Police to investigate who made the reports and to say so publicly. An investigation has begun, and we have cooperated with it.

Section 94 of the BNSS allows a police officer to require a person, by written order, to produce documents needed for an investigation. We complied because this notice is confined to the records of an episode in which we are the affected party. The material was furnished without prejudice to our rights, including the liberty the High Court gave us. If we are asked for anything more, we will look at each request on its own terms, take legal advice and tell you what we can.

Can the police log in to your Tinder, Grindr, or Signal?

Our investigation, published on 11 November, examines tenders from Delhi Police and state forensic science labs, with a list of 422 items. Among them:

1) Remote access tokens (digital keys that open your accounts without a password) for dating apps and encrypted services such as ProtonMail and Signal

2) AI that sorts your photos by person and scans them across 14 categories, including tattoos, gender, and age

Police and forensic labs no longer use these tools only where an FIR is registered. At recent Delhi protests, protesters' phones were taken and never returned.

Foreign surveillance tech, and no rule of law to check it. Let us resist India as a Stasiland.

Statement : Meta told the Home Ministry it acted against 61,000 posts in the fortnight after Chalo Sansad. IFF calls for the record to be made public.

New Delhi, 13 November 2026

Meta has told the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the cybercrime arm of the Ministry of Home Affairs, that it acted on more than 61,000 Facebook and Instagram posts it classified as violent and inciteful between 25 July and 7 August 2026, @ThePrintIndia reported on 12 November. That is about three posts a minute for 14 days. The period begins on the day the Education Minister resigned and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ended its protest at Jantar Mantar, five days after police used tear gas and a lathi charge against its Chalo Sansad march.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the absence of any public account of this action. Meta disclosed the figure to the Home Ministry at a meeting on 21 August, and it became public only because the minutes were filed in the Supreme Court's suo motu proceedings on digital arrest scams.. In IFF's assessment, the minutes record direct pressure from the Ministry of Home Affairs on the content Meta carries.

As per the report in The Print a meeting was chaired by Rajesh Kumar, I4C's chief executive, and followed reviews by the Union Home Secretary, a parliamentary committee and a court-monitored committee on digital arrests. Its scope was wider than financial fraud. 

According to ThePrint, I4C sought an in-person briefing on "how the algorithm amplifies or suppresses specific content and viral accounts", an analysis of bot networks across prominent handles, and Meta's draft guidelines on deepfakes and re-uploaded content for review.
The minutes, as reported, do not state what the 61,000 posts concerned. It is not known which agency, if any, flagged them, or which law or company rule Meta applied. I4C itself did not accept aggregate figures when Meta cited 70 lakh pieces of content removed, it asked for examples with links. Users and the public are entitled to the same detail.

Complaints received by IFF show what was being restricted on Instagram as the period began. Here we are relying on our own inbound queries and requests for pro-bono help and legal assistance.

1) On 23 July, a story about the protests shared by a private account with 137 followers was made unavailable in India through what Instagram described as "an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021.

2) On 24 July, a reel by the journalist Ila Kazmi showing a Delhi Police facial recognition van scanning protesters at Jantar Mantar was withheld on a notice from "The Government of India / Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", which referred her to the Government of India for any questions. The Delhi High Court has directed the Home Ministry, the IT Ministry, the Delhi Police and Meta to produce the notice and will next hear the case on 17 November.

3) On 28 July, three days after the minister's resignation, Instagram withheld a video published on 15 June by the current-affairs page Unmutezone under the title "Why Modi Can't Ask Dharmendra Pradhan to Resign?". Its editor reported that a second video was blocked on 3 August.

Press reports describe similar restrictions. Newslaundry reported that an interview by the journalist Yaqut Ali with a former CJP spokesperson, posted on 26 July, was blocked in India within minutes, and that Facebook reels on the protests by the creator Jyoti Yadav, including an interview with AAP's Sanjay Singh, were restricted. It later reported restrictions on Instagram posts by Scroll and The Hindu about pellet-gun victims in Kashmir. None of this content is violent or inciteful, and Meta has not said whether it forms part of the figure.

The Home Ministry is involved at each stage from notices under Section 79(3)(b) reach platforms through the Sahyog portal, which I4C operates where close to 1.95 lakh blocking orders were issued to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026, most of them through the portal, and Meta has integrated its systems with it so that flagged content can be restricted without human review. On 27 July the Delhi Police, which reports to the Home Ministry, was reported to have directed platforms to remove posts it considered offensive to the Prime Minister. Meta's transparency report lists violence and incitement among the categories that I4C refers to it. A ministry that operates this channel and also reviews Meta's enforcement figures and algorithm is supervising online speech.

We regret to state that the Supreme Court's own proceedings have provided an avenue for such censorship without sufficient checks and balances. In the suo motu digital arrest case, in which it directed intermediaries to place their proposals before I4C, and in the Just Rights for Children Alliance matters, in which it indicated that platforms may lose safe harbour, the Court has largely acted as a facilitator of executive action rather than as an adjudicator of its constitutional limits. The objectives of curbing fraud and protecting children are legitimate, but the supervision they have enabled now extends to lawful speech and results in censorship without legal authority.

These restrictions do not have a basis in law and often executive rulemaking is being used to circumvent the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Section 79(3)(b) sets a condition for a platform's immunity and in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court confined it to court orders and government notifications within Article 19(2). The power to block lies in Section 69A, which requires written reasons, committee review and, following Tanul Thakur (2022), a copy of the order and a hearing for the author. Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules requires each intimation to state reasons, the provision, the unlawful act and the URL, and to be reviewed monthly by a Secretary-rank officer. These requirements cannot be met through an automated integration with a three-hour deadline, whatever share of the 61,000 posts came through Sahyog.

Further, we state that while it may constitute a category of harmful speech, "Violent and inciteful" is not a ground for state mandated censorship under Article 19(2). Shreya Singhal protects discussion and advocacy and permits restriction only at the stage of incitement; a video asking why a minister has not resigned is discussion. Nor is there any clear statutory basis for I4C to perform the function of review a platform's content guidelines or to ask which accounts its algorithm promotes.

Our demands

1) The Ministry of Home Affairs must publish the minutes of its meetings with Meta in 2026 and state how many of the 61,000 posts were flagged by I4C, the Delhi Police or any other agency through Sahyog.

2) Meta must publish a breakdown of the 61,000 posts by the rule or law applied, the action taken and the requesting authority, and give each affected user the notice on which it acted. Further monthly breakdowns with qualitative disclosure is necesary.

3) I4C must withdraw its requests to review Meta's draft guidelines and to be briefed on its algorithm. Oversight of this kind requires a law made by Parliament and may only be performed by an independent regulatory body with a clear mandate and objective.

4) The Union Government must publish the monthly Secretary-level reviews under Rule 3(1)(d) for July and August 2026.

5) Meta must end the automatic execution of government and police flags in India and provide human review, a reasoned notice and an opportunity to respond before any restriction.

Users whose posts or accounts were restricted in India in July or August 2026 may write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of each notice.
